steps.title: CREATE TABLE: a folder and a log, no data
steps.plain: Creating a Delta table writes no data at all. It writes the first commit, _delta_log/00000000000000000000.json, holding the protocol version and the metaData (schema, partition columns, settings). The table is empty because no 'add' action has named any file yet.

inputs.text: CREATE TABLE shop.orders (order_id INT, customer STRING, status STRING, amount_inr DECIMAL(10,2)) USING delta

files.summary: 0 Parquet file(s) on disk · 0 live in the current version

steps.title: INSERT: Parquet files first, then one commit
steps.plain: The rows are written into Parquet files first: 2 of them, because this Spark ran 2 tasks and each task writes its own file. Then commit 1 is written with one 'add' per file, carrying its size and statistics (row count, min and max of every column). Until that commit file exists, nobody can see the rows: the commit is the moment the data appears.

files.summary: 2 Parquet file(s) on disk · 2 live in the current version

steps.title: Another INSERT: the table is the sum of live files
steps.plain: Commit 2 adds 2 more file(s). The table you query is simply every file that has been added and not yet removed. Count the live files in the files panel; together they hold five rows.

files.summary: 4 Parquet file(s) on disk · 4 live in the current version

steps.title: UPDATE one row: the whole file is rewritten
steps.plain: Parquet files are never edited. To change one row, Delta reads the file that holds it and writes a new file with every row of the old one, one of them changed. Commit 3: 1 remove, 1 add, 2 row(s) written to change 1. The old file stays on disk for time travel. That is copy-on-write.

inputs.text: UPDATE shop.orders SET status = 'paid' WHERE order_id = 1003

files.summary: 5 Parquet file(s) on disk · 4 live in the current version

rows: numAddedFiles=1, numUpdatedRows=1, numRemovedFiles=1, numRemovedBytes=1236, numCopiedRows=1, numDeletionVectorsAdded=0, numAddedBytes=1267

steps.title: DELETE one row
steps.plain: Deleting also works on whole files: the file holding order 1004 held only that row, so commit 4 just removes it: 1 remove, no add, nothing rewritten. Files panel: 6 Parquet file(s) on disk · 3 live in the current version. The files that are no longer live stay on disk so old versions can still be read.

files.summary: 6 Parquet file(s) on disk · 3 live in the current version

steps.title: Read an old version
steps.plain: To read version 1, Delta replays commits 0 and 1 only: the files they added and did not remove. Those files are still on disk, so yesterday's table comes back exactly, with order 1004 and the old status of 1003.

inputs.text: SELECT * FROM shop.orders VERSION AS OF 1

files.summary: 6 Parquet file(s) on disk · 3 live in the current version

logs: time travel: read version 1 by replaying commits 0 and 1

steps.title: Ten commits later: a checkpoint
steps.plain: Replaying hundreds of JSON files would get slow, so every 10 commits Delta writes a checkpoint: one Parquet file holding the whole table state at that version, plus _last_checkpoint pointing at it. A reader now starts from the checkpoint and replays only the JSON commits after it.

steps.title: RESTORE: going back is a new commit
steps.plain: RESTORE does not delete history. It writes a new commit (version 11) that removes the files that are live now and re-adds the files that were live in version 2. The table looks like version 2, and you could still restore to version 10.

inputs.text: RESTORE TABLE shop.orders TO VERSION AS OF 2

steps.title: Two writers append at the same time: both win
steps.plain: Both writers read the same version, write their own Parquet file, then race to create the next commit file. Creating a commit file is all-or-nothing: one gets version 2, the other finds it taken, checks that the winner only appended (nothing it read changed), and simply commits as version 3. No locks, no lost rows.

inputs.text:
-- at the same moment, in two sessions:
INSERT INTO shop.w VALUES (4,'placed')   -- writer A
INSERT INTO shop.w VALUES (5,'placed')   -- writer B

files.summary: 4 Parquet file(s) on disk · 4 live in the current version

logs: two appends at once: A committed, B committed

steps.title: Two writers change the same row: one fails
steps.plain: This time both writers UPDATE order 1. Each reads the table to find the row (on an unpartitioned table, that read covers every file). The first to commit wins. The other then sees that the winner added a file its own read would have had to include, so its result might be wrong: it fails with ConcurrentAppendException instead of silently overwriting. Recorded: writer B failed on attempt 1. Look at the files panel: the loser had already written its Parquet file, which no commit names. It is an orphan: no version will ever read it, and VACUUM deletes it later. The fix is to retry (re-read and re-apply), partition or cluster so writers touch different files, or give each table one writer.

inputs.text:
-- at the same moment:
UPDATE shop.w SET status = 'paid'      WHERE order_id = 1   -- writer A
UPDATE shop.w SET status = 'cancelled' WHERE order_id = 1   -- writer B

steps.title: A bigger file, deletion vectors on
steps.plain: A copy of the table with 2,000 rows in one file, created with delta.enableDeletionVectors = true. Look at the metaData configuration in commit 0.

inputs.text:
CREATE TABLE shop.orders_dv (...) TBLPROPERTIES ('delta.enableDeletionVectors' = 'true');
INSERT INTO shop.orders_dv SELECT ... FROM range(0, 2000)

files.summary: 2 Parquet file(s) on disk · 2 live in the current version

logs: orders_dv: 2,000 rows in one file, deletion vectors on

steps.title: DELETE one row: nothing rewritten
steps.plain: With deletion vectors, Delta does not rewrite the file holding order 5007 (about a thousand rows). It writes a tiny deletion vector saying 'this row of this file is deleted', and commits a remove and re-add of the same file with the vector attached (1 file re-added with a vector attached, 0 rows of new data written). Readers skip the marked row. Took 1633 ms here. Compare with the copy-on-write UPDATE in the first scenario.

steps.title: UPDATE one row: mark the old, write the new
steps.plain: An UPDATE becomes 'mark the old row deleted' plus 'write the new row into a small new file'. Fast writes; the cost moves to reads, which must apply the vectors, until OPTIMIZE (or a purge) rewrites the file cleanly.

steps.title: 300 tiny files
steps.plain: 300,000 events written as 300 small files (about a thousand rows each), the way streaming or many small batches leave a table. A query for one customer has to list, open and read every file: it took 777 ms on this laptop.

inputs.text:
spark.range(0, 300000)...repartition(300).write.format('delta').saveAsTable('shop.events')
SELECT count(*), sum(amount) FROM shop.events WHERE customer = 'C-7'

files.summary: 300 Parquet file(s) on disk · 300 live in the current version

steps.title: OPTIMIZE: compact into a few big files
steps.plain: OPTIMIZE reads the small files and writes a few large ones, then commits one 'remove' for each small file and an 'add' for each new one. Same rows, same answer. The same query now took 278 ms instead of 777 ms. The 300 old files stay on disk until VACUUM.

files.summary: 301 Parquet file(s) on disk · 1 live in the current version

logs: after OPTIMIZE: query took 278 ms (was 777 ms)

steps.title: VACUUM: delete files no version needs now
steps.plain: VACUUM deletes Parquet files that are no longer live and are older than the retention period (7 days by default). Here the retention was set to 0 hours, which Delta refuses unless a safety check is switched off. Before: 12 Parquet file(s) on disk · 4 live in the current version. Now only live files remain on disk.

inputs.text:
SET spark.databricks.delta.retentionDurationCheck.enabled = false;   -- never do this in production
VACUUM shop.orders RETAIN 0 HOURS

files.summary: 4 Parquet file(s) on disk · 4 live in the current version

numAddedFiles=0, numRemovedFiles=1, numRemovedBytes=1260, numCopiedRows=0, numDeletionVectorsAdded=0, numDeletedRows=1, numAddedBytes=0

logs: vacuum with 0 hours retention (the safety check had to be switched off first)

steps.title: Time travel after VACUUM: the files are gone
steps.plain: The log still lists version 4, but the files it needs were deleted. Reading it fails. (Version 1 would still work: RESTORE made its files live again, so VACUUM kept them.) That is why the default retention is 7 days and the safety check exists: VACUUM sets how far back you can travel, and long-running readers or streams may still need older files.
